sentence: Measure it: the air on one square centimeter weighs about a kilogram.
claim: Standard sea-level air pressure is 1013.25 hPa, and that pressure is (approximately) the weight of the air above: about 10.1 N, the weight of about 1.03 kg, on each square centimetre.
note: NOAA excerpt: 'The standard pressure at sea-level is 1013.25 in both millibars (mb) and hectopascal (hPa).' Penn State METEO 3 (https://www.e-education.psu.edu/meteo3/print/book/export/html/2000), excerpt: surface pressure 'is approximately the weight of the air in a column that extends from a fixed area on the ground to the top of the atmosphere', about 14.7 pounds per square inch. Arithmetic: 101,325 Pa × 10⁻⁴ m² = 10.13 N; / 9.81 m/s² = 1.033 kg ('about a kilogram'). 14.7 lb/in² = 1.03 kg/cm² agrees.

claim: With the air around the drink pumped below the pressure a mouth can reach inside the straw, no sip lifts the drink: a straw needs air pressing on the drink.
source_title: A Moment of Science (WFIU/WTIU, Indiana Public Media), Air pressure and drinking straws
note: Excerpt: a straw works because of atmospheric pressure, not suction; lowering the pressure inside the straw lets the air pressing on the drink push the liquid up; a straw wouldn't work in space, where there is no atmospheric pressure. 'A more accurate description would be to say that the atmospheric pressure is pushing the liquid up the straw.' The jar (the episode's change) is reasoned from the same mechanism: the mouth, outside the jar, can bring the straw's inside down only to about 900 hPa (c8); once the jar is pumped below that, the drink's surface is pressed less than the straw's inside and no sip lifts it. The scene pumps the jar to 100 hPa (the spine reads it), well above water's 23 hPa vapour pressure (c7), so the drink doesn't boil there.

sentence: In sixteen forty-four, Evangelista Torricelli saw why.
claim: In 1644 Evangelista Torricelli explained the limit of suction pumps by the weight of the air, with his mercury column held up by atmospheric pressure and a vacuum above it.
source_title: APS News, This Month in Physics History: Torricelli demonstrates the existence of a vacuum (October 2012)
note: APS excerpt: well diggers' pumps could lift water only about ten meters; Galileo died in 1642 with the problem unsolved; in 1644 Torricelli inverted a mercury-filled tube about a meter long; the mercury settled about 76 cm above the dish, held by atmospheric pressure, with a vacuum above. Some accounts credit Vincenzo Viviani with performing the experiment (an IMSc paper in the same search); the line says Torricelli 'saw why', which every account agrees on.

sentence: We live at the bottom of an ocean of air, and it presses on everything.
claim: Torricelli wrote to Michelangelo Ricci on 11 June 1644: 'Noi viviamo sommersi nel fondo d'un pelago d'aria' ('we live submerged at the bottom of an ocean of air'); the air's weight presses on every surface.
note: Search excerpt: the quotation, its Italian and the letter's date (11 June 1644, to Ricci); an English translation of the letter at https://web.lemoyne.edu/Giunta/torr.html (found in the same search). The narration paraphrases it (no quotation marks on screen). 'Presses on everything': the pressure acts on every surface (NOAA JetStream fast facts: the air pushes equally on all sides of an object, https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/ll-engagement, search excerpt).

sentence: A sip lowers the pressure inside the straw, and the air outside pushes the drink up.
claim: Sipping lowers the pressure inside the straw; the atmosphere pressing on the drink pushes it up the straw.
source_title: A Moment of Science (WFIU/WTIU, Indiana Public Media), Air pressure and drinking straws
note: Excerpt: a straw works because of atmospheric pressure, not suction; lowering the pressure inside the straw lets the air pressing on the drink push the liquid up; a straw wouldn't work in space, where there is no atmospheric pressure. 'A more accurate description would be to say that the atmospheric pressure is pushing the liquid up the straw.' Arithmetic for the scene: lifting the drink 20 cm needs 998 × 9.81 × 0.20 = 1,958 Pa ≈ 20 hPa, so the spine goes 1013 → 993 hPa.

sentence: The water stops near ten meters.
claim: Even a perfect vacuum above it can't lift water higher than the atmosphere's push supports: about 10.3 m with no vapour at all, about 10.1 m for water at 20 °C; suction pumps of the 1600s stalled near ten meters.
source_title: APS News, This Month in Physics History: Torricelli demonstrates the existence of a vacuum (October 2012)
note: Excerpt: pumps could lift water only about ten meters. Arithmetic: h = p/(ρg) = 101,325 / (998.2 × 9.81) = 10.35 m with no vapour (10.33 m with ρ = 1000); with 20 °C water's vapour pressure 2,339 Pa (c7) above it: (101,325 − 2,339) / (998.2 × 9.81) = 10.11 m, where the scene stops. 'Near ten meters' covers both. Chemistry World (https://www.chemistryworld.com/opinion/torricellis-barometer/1017293.article) gives the 18-braccia historical limit; the Science ABC explainer in the same search gives 10.33 m theoretical and about 10.1 m for 20 °C water. 'A perfect pump' is said aloud. The scene's storeys are 3.4 m, the straw's top at 10.6 m, so the water stops just under the pump.

sentence: At the top, room-temperature water boils.
claim: Water boils when the pressure on it falls to its vapour pressure, about 2.34 kPa at 20 °C; above the column only that vapour remains, so the water at the top boils unheated.
source_title: Boston University physics demonstrations, How to boil water at room temperature
note: BU excerpt: 'The definition of the boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which the vapor pressure of the water equals the external pressure... The vacuum pump is used to lower the external pressure until it equals the vapor pressure of the water. At that point, the water boils - at room temperature!' Vapour pressure at 20 °C: 2.3388 kPa, LibreTexts reference table S3 (https://chem.libretexts.org/Ancillary_Materials/Reference/Reference_Tables/Solvents/S3%3A_Vapor_Pressure_of_Water), search excerpt. The spine reads 23 hPa at the top. 'Room-temperature' assumes a room near 20 °C.

claim: Healthy adults' strongest suction at the mouth (maximal inspiratory pressure) is typically about 70–125 cm of water, so lungs alone could hold water in a straw only about 0.7–1.25 m up.
source_title: Determinants of maximal inspiratory pressure. The Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (PubMed)
note: Excerpts: mean MIP 101 cmH2O for men, 72 for women (Baltimore); 75 ± 27 cmH2O (Manizales, Colombia, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4001942/); a Singapore study median 95 (IQR 73–122). Arithmetic: a pressure of 100 cm of water holds a 1.0 m column of water, by the unit's definition. The sentence answers 'Your lungs?' ({-}). The scene's spine shows 1013 − 98 = 915 hPa for the lungs' best (≈ 100 cm of water).

sentence: So does ten point three meters of water.
claim: A column of water 1 cm² across and 10.3 m tall weighs about 1.03 kg, the same as the air above each square centimetre at sea level.
source_title: Penn State METEO 3: Introductory Meteorology, air pressure
note: Arithmetic: 1 cm² × 1033 cm = 1033 cm³ of water at 1 g/cm³ = 1.033 kg, equal to c1's 1.033 kg; equivalently 101,325 / (1000 × 9.81) = 10.33 m. The source is c1's second one, for the air's side of the balance.

claim: A straw doesn't pull the drink up; the atmosphere pushes it.
source_title: A Moment of Science (WFIU/WTIU, Indiana Public Media), Air pressure and drinking straws
note: Excerpt: a straw works because of atmospheric pressure, not suction; lowering the pressure inside the straw lets the air pressing on the drink push the liquid up; a straw wouldn't work in space, where there is no atmospheric pressure. 'A more accurate description would be to say that the atmospheric pressure is pushing the liquid up the straw.'

sentence: You thin the air inside, and the sky pushes.
claim: Sipping lowers the air pressure inside the straw, and the weight of the air above the drink pushes it up.
source_title: A Moment of Science (WFIU/WTIU, Indiana Public Media), Air pressure and drinking straws
note: Excerpt: a straw works because of atmospheric pressure, not suction; lowering the pressure inside the straw lets the air pressing on the drink push the liquid up; a straw wouldn't work in space, where there is no atmospheric pressure. 'A more accurate description would be to say that the atmospheric pressure is pushing the liquid up the straw.' 'The sky' is the air column of c1 (Penn State).
